name: DOT Hazardous Materials Transportation, Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description: The Department of Transportation requires each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation to describe the material on a properly prepared shipping paper. (49 CFR 172.22). Except for hazardous wastes, there is no specific form or format for hazardous material shipping papers. A shipping paper may include a shipping order, bill of lading, manifest or other shipping document. The detailed requirements for shipping papers are found in 49 CFR 172.200.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
The Bill of Lading

This is the basic shipping paper used for transportation by common carriers for hire. It is a contract between the shipper and the carrier to perform delivery service and it outlines the specific responsibilities of each party. The shipper must prepare the bill of lading in accordance with the regulations if the material is hazardous. The bill of lading also carries a very important declaration, the shipper's certification. The certification states that the shipment was prepared strictly in accordance with the regulations. The shipper acknowledges responsibility for compliance when this statement is signed.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
The following is a list of information that will appear on a bill of lading, if required.

  1. The proper shipping name
  2. Technical name for NOS Technical name for NOS
  3. The hazard class number
  4. The UN or NA ID Number
  5. Packing Group I, II, or III
  6. Quantity (volume or weight)
  7. The word "POISON"(PGIII)
  8. Exemption Number
  9. Shipper's certification
  10. 24-hour emergency number
  11. Hazardous substance name
  12. Signature

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
The Waste Manifest

This is the correct shipping paper for generators of hazardous waste required by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) when hazardous waste is transported. It is permitted as a shipping paper by the DOT under the provisions of 49 CFR 172.205.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Shipping Papers

The shipping papers must conform to many requirements. In general, if hazardous materials and non hazardous materials are shipped together and described on the same shipping paper, the hazardous materials entries

  • must be listed first, or
  • must be entered in a contrasting color, or
  • must be identified with the letter "X" placed in the hazardous materials (HM) column.

The entries must be legible and printed in English and each of the pages must be numbered (i.e. page 1 of 4, page 2 of 4).

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Each hazardous material must be described accurately on the shipping papers. The language and sequence of the separate elements of the "basic description" are found in 49 CFR 172.202 .The "basic description" must include

  1. The proper shipping name,
  2. Hazard class or division,
  3. UN identification number, and
  4. Packing group.

These are found in columns 2, 3, 4, and 5 of the HMT respectively. The preferred sequence of the basic description begins with the UN number, followed by the proper shipping name, hazard class and finally packing group.

For example "UN 1203, Gasoline, 3, PG II",

This sequence is required on international shipments and on shipments by air, beginning January 1, 2007.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description: The traditional sequence which begins with the Proper shipping name, followed by the hazard class, UN number and packing group will be allowed for domestic shipments only until January 1, 2013. The DOT final rule published December 29, 2006 adopts the new sequence but allows for a six-year phase-in period.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Thetotal quantityof the hazardous material being shipped must be shown before or after the basic description on the shipping paper, and include the units of measure (i.e. pounds, gallons, kilograms). In addition, for transportation by aircraft, the total quantity per package must be shown as net mass. For example, UN 1263, Paint, 3, PG II, 5 fiberboard boxes x 5L each.

The letters RQ need to be on the bill of lading before or after the basic description if the material is also a hazardous substance.

The number and type of packages (mandatory after 10/1/07) must also be included.(For example, "12 drums").

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
As of January 9, 2006, shippersmust retain a copy of shipping papers for a period of two (2) yearsafter the material is accepted by the initial carrier. For hazardous wastes, the manifest must be retained for at least 3 years.

An emergency telephone number, which is monitored at all times the shipment is being transported, must be on the shipping papers immediately after the hazardous material description.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description: The basic description for our drum of flammable liquid, toxic, n.o.s. would include the following:

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
The basic description for our drum of flammable liquid, toxic, n.o.s. would include the following:

"UN1992, Flammable liquid, toxic, n.o.s. (contains Toluene, Tetrabromoethane), 3, PG II" (Sequence required by IATA, DOT preferred sequence with six-year phase-in)

"Flammable liquid, toxic, n.o.s. (contains Toluene, Tetrabromoethane), 3, UN1992 PG II"

A technical name was needed because the proper shipping name selected had a "G" in Column 1 or the HMT. This means that a technical name for each of the hazardous components of the mixture must be included in the basic description. We have classified the material and have selected a description (Flammable liquid, toxic, n.o.s. etc.).

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Shippers Certification

Each hazardous material shipping paper also requires the "shippers certification" to be printed on the shipping paper. The required text is found 49 CFR 172.204.

  1. This is to certify that the above-named materials are properly classified, described, packaged, marked, and labeled and are in proper condition for transportation according to the applicable regulations of the Department of Transportation.
  2. I hereby declare that the content of this consignment are fully and accurately described above by the proper shipping name and are classified, packaged, marked and labeled/placcarded and are in all respects in proper condition for transport according to applicable international and national government regulation.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
A new certification statement replaces the requirement for the air eligibility mark on packages being transported by air. The text for the certification statement is as follows, with the new text added.

"I hereby declare that the contents of this consignment are fully and accurately described above by the proper shipping name and are classified, packaged, marked and labeled/placarded and are in all respects in proper condition for transport according to applicable international and national government regulation.I declare that all of the applicable air transport requirements have been met."

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Hazardous Substances

Since this material consists of a material also listed in Appendix A, we need to determine whether the final mixture is a "hazardous substance." To do this we need to address two things: the first is "what is the reportable quantity for Toluene in Appendix A. The second is "what is the capacity of the container we are using? The listed RQ for Toluene is 1,000 lb. If the answer to our second question is a tank truck then the shipment also qualifies as a hazardous substance. This is because the quantity of the Toluene in the tank truck will most likely exceed the 1,000 lb RQ. The letters RQ must be inserted in the basic description if the material qualifies as a hazardous substance.

On the other hand, a single 55-gallon drum would NOT qualify as a hazardous substance, for the obvious reason that the drum could not contain 1,000 lbs of toluene. Therefore the drum shipment would not have to have the "RQ" indicated on the bill of lading.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
HOW TO PROPERLY PREPARE A BILL OF LADING

  1. Insert full name of carrier (transporter)
  2. Insert full name of consignee (customer)
  3. Indicate number of pieces (units) of freight, i.e., drum, cartons, etc.
  4. Enter an "X" in the HM column to denote hazardous material.
  5. Enter "RQ" in the HM column if a hazardous substance.
  6. Enter full hazardous material basic description.
  7. Include technical names, if required, in the basic description.
  8. Enter the words "Marine Pollutant", if required.
  9. Include a 24-hour emergency response telephone number.
  10. Sign the bill of lading.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Loading and Bracing

One of the most important requirements in making a safe shipment is to pay special attention to this activity. It is often overlooked and thought by some people, to be a carrier responsibility. The fact is that it is the shipper's responsibility to properly secure the shipment in the carrier's vehicle. The regulation is quite specific and reads as follows: (49 CFR 173.30 177.834)

Sec. 173.30 - Loading unloading transport vehicles

"A person who loads or unloads hazardous materials into or from a transport vehicle shall comply with the applicable loading and unloading requirements of Parts 174, 175, 176, and 177."

It is the shipper, or whomever performs the function of a shipper, who is responsible for this important function. If your shipment is being made by truck, then Part 177 applies; if by rail, Part 174, etc. The requirements of Part 177.834 are also quite explicit.

Sec. 177.834 - General requirements

(a)"Any packaging not permanently attached to a motor vehicle, which contains any Class 3, Class 2, Class 8, Class 6.1 or Class 7 materials must be secured against movement within the vehicle on which it is being transported, under conditions normally incident to transportation.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
In addition to these requirements, a special provision for Class 6.1(Toxic/Poison) materials applies in 49 CFR 177.841. It reads as follows:

"A package bearing a POISON or TOXIC label may not be transported in the same motor vehicle with material that is marked as or known to be foodstuff, feed or any edible material intended for consumption by humans or animals unless the poisonous material is packaged in accordance with the Hazardous Materials Regulations and is overpacked in a metal drum as specified in 49 CFR 173.25(c)."

In addition, a material bearing a KEEP AWAY FROM FOOD label, must be separated from foodstuffs as required by 49 CFR 177.841(e)(3).

Sec 173.159- Batteries, wet

Specific requirements for packaging electric storage batteries are found in 49 CFR173.159. In general, batteries must be protected against short circuits and firmly secured to skids or pallets capable of withstanding the shocks normally incident to transportation. Other requirements are dependent upon the size and type of batteries. Be sure to review this section when shipping batteries.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Step 8 Emergency Response Information (49 CFR 172.600)

In addition to the emergency response telephone number on the shipping paper, emergency response information must accompany hazardous materials shipments during transportation and be maintained at facilities where hazardous materials are loaded for transportation, stored incidental to transportation, or otherwise handled during any phase of transportation. This information must be available and may be in the form of the DOT Emergency Response Guidebook, an MSDS, or another document associated with the shipping papers and be immediately accessible by the driver of the vehicle. It must include:

  1. The basic description and technical name of the hazardous material,
  2. Immediate hazards to health,
  3. Risks of fire or explosion,
  4. Immediate precautions to be taken in the event of an incident or accident,
  5. Immediate methods of handling spills or leaks with no fire, and
  6. Preliminary first aid measures.

A 24-hour emergency response telephone number must be listed on each hazardous material shipping paper. This number must be answered by a knowledgeable person with comprehensive emergency response information at hand, for the materials being shipped, or by someone who has immediate access to such a person. The number must be monitored at all times while the hazardous material is in transportation.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Step 9 Placarding Requirements(49CFR 172.500)

This requirement is simply stated in the regulations as follows; "each person who offers for transportation or transports any hazardous materials ...shall comply with the applicable placarding requirements of this subpart." Placards must clearly communicate the hazard of the material being transported. This information is crucial during an emergency. Placards must be displayed on each side and each end of bulk packaging, freight container, unit load device, transport vehicle and rail car carrying hazardous materials. Some materials are excepted from the placarding rules including:

  • Shipments of INFECTIOUS substances,
  • Materials re-classified as ORM-D,
  • Shipments offered as LIMITED QUANTITIES,
  • Certain MATERIALS of TRADE,
  • All SMALL QUANTITY shipments, and
  • COMBUSTIBLE liquids in non-bulk packagings

Placards may be one of three varieties; they may either be worded, wordless or numbered. In general, the worded placards are used on transport vehicles, in much the same way as DOT labels are used on packages. Their purpose is exactly the same. However, with the exception of radioactive materials of class 7, the text, i.e., words of a hazard, are not required. This provision is in keeping with the international labeling and placarding scheme where "wordless" is the norm. Either worded or wordless placards may be used.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
The numbered placards are useful to combine the marking AND placarding requirements with a single application. For instance, the identification number "1992" is used on packages, as we have seen.

Shippers may use "numbered" placards for their shipments (see illustration), when the total weight of a single hazardous material on the truck exceeds 4000 kg (8820 lb). This requirement is essentially a "marking" requirement, not a placarding requirement and was discussed under the marking requirements.

Generally, "any truck transporting over 1,000 lb. gross weight of non-bulk packages of hazardous materials must be placarded." These placards must be:

  1. Displayed on each side and each end of vehicle,
  2. Visible from the direction they face, and
  3. Mounted with words and/or numbers displayed horizontally.

The basic placarding requirements are associated with two Tables. One is called TABLE 1 and consists of the most sensitive of hazardous materials, including EXPLOSIVES, POISON GASES, INHALATION-HAZARD liquids, and RADIOACTIVE materials. ANY quantity of these requires placards.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
TABLE 2 consists of the rest of the hazardous materials classes that need placarding. Materials in Table 2 are required to be placarded only when the gross weight of all the hazardous materials on board is 454 kg (1001 lbs) or more. Shipments of more than one hazard class may require more than one placard. The following placarding rules apply to non-bulk packages containing hazardous materials listed in TABLE 2.

A truck loaded with 9,000 lb. of flammable liquids (class 3), 2,000 lb. of corrosives (class 8) and 2,000 lb. of poisons (class 6.1) could be placarded as shown. Optionally, a placard for each class is permitted.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Step 10 Security

Awareness Training

All hazmat employeesmust receive training that provides anawarenessof the security risks associated with hazardous materials transportation and methods to enhance hazardous materials transportation security. The training must be provided at the employee’s first scheduled recurrent training after March 25, 2003. Hazmat employees at sites with security plans must receive more in-depth training.

Everyone who is involved in the transportation of hazardous materials should be aware of security issues associated with such transportation. All employees should know that certain people may ask questions or seek to acquire information that could be used to target hazardous materials for criminal or terrorist acts.

The in-depth security training found in 49 CFR 172.704(a)(5) is required only for hazmat employees who handle or perform regulated functions related to the transportation of the materials listed in 49 CFR 172.800(b) or who are responsible for implementing a security plan. These hazmat employees must receive in-depth training on the specific portions of the plan for which they are responsible, including specific security procedures, employee responsibilities, and actions to be taken in the event of a security breach.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Additional resources have been developed by the DOT to assist in enhancing hazardous materials transportation safety and security.

The DOT recently sponsored development of a framework for risk management applicable to the transportation of hazardous materials. The product, designated as the Risk Management Self-Evaluation Framework (RMSEF), provides a basic framework for managing risk as part of the hazardous materials transportation process. RMSEF is a tool for all parties (regulators, shippers, carriers, emergency response personnel, etc.) to look at their operations and consider how they assess and manage risk (http://hazmat.dot.gov/riskmgmt/rmsef/rmsef.htm).

You may want to review the DOT's Hazmat Transportation Security Requirements brochure, Frequently Asked Questions, and training (downloadable from the DOT website or available on CD-ROM, http://hazmat.dot.gov/riskmgmt/hmt/hmt_security.htm).

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Security Plan

In 2003, DOT added a new subchapter to the Hazardous Materials Regulations, 49 CFR 172.800 Security Plans. Individuals shipping one or more of the following hazardous materials must develop and adhere to a security plan for hazardous materials that conforms to the requirements of these new regulations:

  1. A highway route-controlled quantity of a Class 7 (radioactive) material, as defined in § 173.403 of this subchapter, in a motor vehicle, rail car, or freight container
  2. More than 25 kg (55 pounds) of a Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 (explosive) material in a motor vehicle, rail car, or freight container
  3. More than one L (1.06 qt) per package of a material poisonous by inhalation, as defined in § 171.8 of this subchapter, that meets the criteria for Hazard Zone A, as specified in § § 173.116(a) or 173.133(a) of this subchapter
  4. A shipment of a quantity of hazardous materials in a bulk packaging having a capacity equal to or greater than 13,248 L (3,500 gallons) for liquids or gases or more than 13.24 cubic meters (468 cubic feet) for solids
  5. A shipment in other than a bulk packaging of 2,268 kg (5,000 pounds) gross weight or more of one class of hazardous materials for which placarding of a vehicle, rail car, or freight container is required for that class under the provisions of Subpart F of this part
  6. A select agent or toxin regulated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under 42 CFR Part 73, or
  7. A quantity of hazardous material that requires placarding under the provisions of subpart F of this part.

slides.title: Shipping Papers, Emergency Response & Placarding
slides.description:
Individuals receiving hazardous materials, but not shipping them, are not subject to the security plan requirements.

A security plan must include an assessment of possible transportation security risks for shipments of the hazardous materials covered by the plan and appropriate measures to address the assessed risks. At a minimum, a security plan must include the following elements:

  1. Personnel security: Measures to confirm information provided by job applicants hired for positions that involve access to and handling of the hazardous materials covered by the security plan.
  2. Unauthorized access: Measures to address the possibility that unauthorized persons may gain access to the hazardous materials covered by the security plan or to transport conveyances being prepared for transportation of the hazardous materials covered by the security plan.
  3. En route security: Measures to address the security risks of shipments of hazardous materials covered by the security plan en route from origin to destination, including shipments stored incidental to movement.

The security plan must be in writing and must be retained for as long as it remains in effect. Copies of the security plan must be available to the employees who are responsible for implementation. The security plan must be revised and updated as necessary to reflect changing circumstances. To avoid unnecessary duplication, security plans that conform to regulations issued by other agencies, or industry organizations may be used to satisfy the requirements in this subpart, provided such security plans address all the requirements specified by DOT in 49 CFR 172.800.
